This camcorder is a simple way for you to share videos with friends and family, make and share mini-movies, capture special moments, or film your next masterpiece for YouTube or Amazon.com.

Pros:
1. The "cool" factor is off the scale. Every time I showed it to somebody, they said "COOL!!!"

2. It uses two AA batteries that are easy to install. There's a latch at the bottom of the camera - one side has a picture of a closed lock, and the other has a picture of an open lock. It doesn't get simpler than that, does it? Push towards the open lock and slide off the panel on the front of the camera from just under the lens. After you put in the batteries, slide the panel back into place and push the latch back to the locked position. You're now ready to start filming.

3. There are very few buttons required to operate the camera. Turning it so that the side with the big red button is facing you, the on/off switch is on the right side of the camera. After powering up, the screen will light up with the Flip logo and then it will indicate that it's ready. At this stage you'll be looking at whatever's in front of you, with a time check at the bottom telling you how much video time you have left.

4. Filming is easy - just press the red button to start, and press it again to stop. The camera will save your creation, tell you how long it is and how much time you have left. You can zoom in and out by pressing the + and - signs on top of and below the red button. The microphone will pick up and record whatever's going on at the time.

5. Playback is a one button operation.

6. Deleting your mistakes is a one button operation.

7. You can scroll through your videos by using the arrow keys to the left and right of the red button.

8. Getting it on your computer is the easiest part. With the red button facing you, pull down on the latch on the left side, and - surprise!!! Out pops a USB arm which you then connect to your computer. Once you're linked up, the Flip Video software will show you the way home. (It takes a while to pop up) Choose the option to view your videos, and agree to the terms and conditions, and then the "Muvee Video Mixing Software" begins loading. This is a one time installation. From there you can easily play, name, edit and share your videos.

9. You can also capture still shots from your videos, but you can't use these when making your movies with the software provided.

10. There is an option for making a movie, where you can arrange your edited videos, choose from a selection of six movie styles and music, or even add your own music. Choose your style, click on the "Make Mix" button, and the computer does the rest. If you're happy with the results, you can save the file.

11. The camera comes with a wrist strap, a velvet drawstring case, and also the necessary cables to connect it to your television for a bigger view. There's also a place to connect a tripod.

12. There is a "Help" feature included with the software.

Cons:
1. Being a simple "point and shoot" camera, the resolution isn't fantastic, but quite good enough for action shots. Forget detail close-ups such as words and logos - zooming in and out will just get you various degrees of blurry.

2. You'll need to be careful with background noise, as the microphone will pick up the sound of your fan or your stomach growling.

3. The video editing capability is limited to the length of the video you want to save, and the order you want to save it. There are no options for titles, fade ins or outs or any bells and whistles. If you're filming yourself giving a speech, you'll pretty much have to get it right in one complete take.

4. As with all videos, if your hands shake, you'll need to get a tripod, or you may make a lot of people seasick.

5. If you have big fingers, you may have some problems with the red button. Once your finger covers the area around the button, you'll have trouble starting and stopping the video. If you can't get it to work, you may have to use just a fingernail, because if you press anywhere other than dead center of the red button it won't start or stop.

Overall, this is a very good camcorder if used for the purpose for which it is intended. It isn't going to make you the next Stanley Kubrick, but it's a good start.

Amanda Richards, October 9, 2007

UPDATE: Six months in, this router has been flawless. AND I've discovered it has its own dynamic DNS support capability. That's a nice feature if you run any sort of server application. So, I continue to be impressed with this product.

---

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

As 'cool' as the cloth covered outer jacket is, this retro look on this cable has a real purpose. Most cables use PVC for the jacket and the dielectric properties will cause some signal distortion when they go through their store/discharge cycle. Granted, the amount of charge a PVC jacket will store and eventually discharge is minute and also will not affect charging. However, many of us use our cables to sync to laptops and other devices and with the cloth jacket this effect is so minimized as to be nominal.

There are other reasons why I awarded the review sample I received five stars. At the top of the list is this cable not only supports charging my Note 3, but also is flawless when it comes to synching it. Not all cables I own will synch (sounds incredible, but unfortunately true), This one will and my guess why it's done so without errors so far is the gold plated connector that do aid in conductivity. Another reason for the five stars is the heavy duty housing for the connectors and how they manage to be both thin enough to be unobtrusive and substantial enough to assure a long service life. There are even strain reliefs on each end of the cable to minimize wear that can eventually cause diminished transmission at the weak points in any USB cable.

Finally, the ends mate perfectly with every device with which I've tried them. I have only tested the micro USB end on my Note 3, but have tested the USB A end on my laptop, various chargers and battery backups and the fits on all are precise.

This IHOME iAV5B COLOR CHANGING BLUETOOTH RECHARGEABLE STEREO SPEAKER SYSTEM FOR AMAZON ECHO DOT adds a colorful light show to my powder room! It’s no space hog—the footprint is only slightly wider than the Echo Dot itself (2nd Generation Dot, see buyer warning note below). The speaker also raises the Dot well above the countertop, so that the Dot’s “active” light ring is much easier to see.

As for the sound, it’s better than the sound from my original Echo (the tall one with built-in speakers). It’s a huge improvement over the tinny Dot speakers. I use the speaker system to play music (from Prime Music, and from my playlist) and environmental sounds (rain, etc.). I also use it as an intercom (“Alexa, Drop in ….”) and for all the usual Alexa tasks (shopping lists, lookup answers, etc.).

The speaker system is very easy to set up. You place your Gen2 Dot into the well, connect it to the internal USB cable, and plug the speaker into a wall outlet using a USB cable and AC adapter. (The cable and adapter are NOT included, but you should already have these—you can use the same ones that came with your Dot.) You then open the Alexa app and use Bluetooth to pair the Dot and the speaker. (If your Dot is already connected to your wireless network, you don’t have to fool with wireless connections at all.)

Once the speaker is plugged in and paired, the buttons on the Dot will turn the power and the mic on and off, and will control the volume. Voice commands will also control the volume. A button on the back of the speaker controls the lightshow (color cycling speed, color changing, on/off). As long as the speaker is charged, you can move it (and the Dot) around your house, and it will operate without being plugged in.

BUYER WARNING NOTE: This speaker system is designed for the 2nd Generation Echo Dot, which has volume buttons on top. The Gen2 Dot drops into a well atop the speaker, and sits flush with the top edge of the speaker. The only hiccup happened when I finished that as the rest of my network went haywire with my smart devices not connecting and reconnecting. I restarted my modem and my primary router and everything appears to be back to operating as normal. I’m not sure what caused the glitch.

I can definitely see a WiFi speed increase in the area of the house that the extender is located and the TV that is plugged into the Ethernet port is streaming perfectly.

I am very pleased with this extender and would recommend it to anyone who needed to extend their WiFi range or provide an Ethernet Port to a device that is too far from their current hub.

After finally needing to retire my last phone with a headphone jack, it was time to try out some of these USBC to 3.5mm adapters. The good news is, it works really well and actually is small enough to leave attached to the end of my favorite set of wired headphones. You're not going to get audiophile quad-dac quality out of it like my old LG phones, but it will drive a normal pair of headphones just fine for music or videos.
HOWEVER, there are a couple of things to note:
1) It seems to support the audio out channels but not the microphone, if your headphones have one. You know how phone earbuds usually have an extra pin for the microphone on the tip (3 rings instead of 2)? I think this doesn't support that. I believe this jack is TRS instead of TRRS. Or even if it IS a TRRS, it's only telling my phone that the left and right audio channels are there. Which leads me to item #2:
2) It tells the phone a headset is connected even if it is not. And I think this also is related to #1, because it doesn't seem to care what's plugged into the other side of it, as soon you plug this adapter into your phone, even empty, the headphones icon shows up and all audio is routed out to the empty 3.5mm jack. Plug something in, you hear the sound. Unplug it, the sound goes nowhere. This is why I'm happy to leave it semi-permanently attached to my earphones, and just considering it an extension of them. You don't want to leave this attached to your phone with nothing plugged in.

In a nutshell, this is great if you want to listen to music. Not if you want to use a wired headset for phone calls.

2006 Volvo S60R with factory HU with Pioneer sound system and 6 cd changer. I watched numerous GROM and non-GROM youtube videos and thought myself prepared. Factory HU removal went delightfully quickly, with my manual transmission in neutral and e-brake on I didn't have to shuffle or wedge it out like some videos suggest who want you to keep changing gears to get it out. That being said I'd recommend putting down a cloth or something to protect your interior from dings during this process. I do not have an interior tool I use an excellent and inexpensive spatula from Ikea (swedes are ingenious). First step was popping out the surround from the shifter. Next 2 T25 hex screws. Next stereo glides out. Process was very fast and left me feeling over confident. Install was a breeze, took 10 seconds. Here's where hell broke loose. All the videos claim "plenty of room behind the stereo to tuck the device". What happened for me was no matter where I stuffed everything back behind, that stupid stereo would NOT fit back into place! I was furious and was using my feet against it when I took a breath, went inside (my dog was watching me from the window with a judgemental look in his eyes), and got a drink of water. Then I went back out and tried to be calm. I now realize that the extras my car has (no factory navigation but extra wires and plugs for back up park assist camera if one is ever installed) were just the tipping point for stuffability to get everything back in. I took my time, tried shoving things more to the left than the right which had always been suggested in videos for the S60, and finally things clicked back in. It was at this point that I was concerned all my shuffling and stuffing may have caused a loose connection so I double checked and tightened clips and plugs and did it again. Thankfully everything went back in again. PS I also drilled a small hole in the back of the storage slot to the left of the stereo for the plug to come out of since its right below where my Spigen magnetic phone mount is in the vent above. Before I did this I really electrical taped the plug into the Grom unit so no amount of time or jiggling would get it loose.

I reconnected the battery, turned the car on, plugged in my phone, set it playing Vast's "I'm dying", turned the stereo's settings to CD mode, and.... some crazy hip hop dance song came blasting out. Thankfully someone had left a CD in the stereo and I was not on the CD changer mode but the CD mode and after removing the disc and switching to the correct mode, wonderful music poured from all the speakers. Stunning quality and so happy Grom exists. I debated installing the full bluetooth aux microphone version but this is all I need. I will say my Note 8's speaker phone quality is apparently not great for callers on the other end but this could be due to my car's elevate exhaust background noise. Maybe one day I'll spring from the version with the mic but I'm very happy with this and don't talk in the car hardly ever.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

Due to my security concerns with WiFi cameras my current security system is completely run through a dedicated computer utilizing the Blue Iris software. While this may seem intimidating to some, it is well worth learning and utilizing for the huge advantages in privacy and security.

I’ve noticed many people have asked if this camera works with a Blue Iris and it does without any issue. Just update to the latest firmware. The remainder of setup within Blue Iris is straightforward. This IPC2387C supports PoE 802.3af and will work with 48V active adapters which are more expensive, but you can also rely on a PoE switch, which in my opinion is a much easier, straightforward option. Something to note, if you plan on powering via a DC cable this is not included.

The fixed lens size of 2.8mm provides decent field of view and the digital zoom is acceptable. The 1/2.8” CMOS 8MP image sensor is decent in low light, certainly not as good as 1/1.8” but I’ve found the low light capabilities average in comparison to other similar cameras. The LEDs must be illuminating objects to provide what is considered “colored night vision” which is misleading.

The camera has a built in microphone that allows for sound recording, though no speaker so two way communication will not be possible with this unit.

In terms of storage, the IPC2387C utilizes H.265 which is currently the best option for video compression. I have had this set up utilizing Blue Iris software which I definitely recommend.

When all things are taken into account this is a solidly build camera, suited to outdoor environments, decent daytime / nighttime resolution, fairly easily mounted, and setup in Blue Iris was reasonably easy and straightforward.

While I would prefer to have pan and tilt capabilities at this price point that is unrealistic. Overall I have been moderately impressed with this budget camera and would recommend it for many security situations.

I have been shooting a Canon 50D DSLR for several years, mostly outside or with stage lighting. Occasionally, I also have been using a small camera-mounted flash, but it is weak and very limited. To improve my flash photography, I decided to try the Mago Speedlight by Pixel. This is an excellent, mid-priced flash with loads of features.

The Mago Speedlight comes with a nice soft case and a fold-out manual which guides you through the setup of the flash and includes screenshots of the back LCD. It also includes a small stand which is great for use in slave mode, and a clip-on flash defuser. The flash uses 4 AA batteries or an external power supply (not provided). It is even upgradable via a USB port hidden in the battery compartment (not tested).

The controls are easy to use after some experimenting. The manual really helps as there are so many features. The buttons are solid and the display is easy to read, with an optional green backlight.

The flash head can be tilted up and down, or rotated left or right. It also includes a built-in defuser and a white card reflector. These are very useful if you are not bouncing the flash off of a ceiling or reflector.

One interesting feature is an LED model light that can be turned on/off easily via a dedicated button. This light is quite bright and very useful for setting up your shots.

I tested the flash on a Canon 50D with 20mm and 50mm lenses and somewhat cooperative subjects (my kids). After learning the controls, I took several excellent pictures.

The flash supports E-TTL mode, manual mode, and multi-flash mode. I tested all three.

To test the multi-flash mode, I set the flash to 5 bursts at 500 HZ and took a picture of fan blades, resulting in a very interesting effect.

As a final test, I put the flash in slave move (S1) and put my old flash on the camera. This flash worked great as a slave flash and I took some interesting pictures using both flashes. I also used S1 mode to slave the this flash to the camera's on-board flash. Note, I did not test the wireless flash mode (a smart slave mode) as I do not have another flash that supports that feature.

This came perilously close to being an angry review of Windows 8 the first week I had the 13, but then I calmed down, learned enough about how to navigate the new OS, and began to enjoy the computer for its own sake. It's a fast, powerful little number with a startlingly quick boot up, something I can't say for any of my other machines. It multi-tasks better than any computer I've ever owned, and I'm not just talking about having Chrome open with a couple of Word documents. I'm talking a couple of graphics-intensive programs plus Spotify, plus a web browser with a lot of open tabs. Basically a bunch of memory hogs couldn't even slow the 13 down, and I am loving that.

Why? Well I'm not a gamer per se, so what's important to me is that I can do the work I do -- I'm a writer, editor, and artist with a lot of social media outlets -- in the way I want to do it, which is often a matter of moving from one program to another, to work in a limited time frame. With music. The 13 can handle everything I throw at it including large graphics files, without a wibble. The games I do play play flawlessly and look terrific.

Specifics: The keyboard is fairly compact, and there's no number pad, which I miss only a little. It has a good feel, which is important for anyone who spends hours typing. The screen is small, obviously, but it's bright and crisp. Graphics look good on this screen, though I have noticed that color is rendered a bit differently than on my other laptops. I haven't tried adjusting it yet. Once I start printing out my art, I'll do any color adjustments I need to do. The sound? I love it. It's clear and warm, nothing tinny or muddy about these speakers.

It comes loaded with some decent software. There's not a lot of bloat here. What you get is useful or genuinely fun, like the Alien FX which tickles me because it allows me to change the lighting theme. Yes, yes, I know that's fru-fru stuff, but I like the shiny. Oh, and a terrabyte HD? I am so there. I have a lot of media files, and that lets me keep them all in one place rather than having to store them on an external hard drive. And speaking of drives, do be aware that there is no optical drive in this unit. If you need one you'll have to get a stand-alone. This isn't a huge hardship, they're not expensive these days. It's just a bit inconvenient.

Look, the bottom line here is that if you can afford a computer just for gaming you can probably afford something bigger and better. But if you also have to use your computer for other things, work, school, a life... this is going to serve you pretty well, in my opinion. If, like me, you want to do graphics work on a laptop (My desktop is ancient and creaky but up to this point was the only machine I had that could support Photoshop effectively.) this is a machine to consider.

I have been using these window alarms for a few months and have found them fairly dependable. These products will not replace a traditional security system but instead are a nice addition to a more advanced security system.

As with any similar product it’s important to have a strong WiFi signal in the location they are placed so they can communicate. I utilize an excellent mesh network so this has not been an issue.

These will send an alert through the app when they detect vibration and the alarm will go off for around 20 seconds. It’s loud and will scare off the majority of intruders.

The sensitivity can not be controlled via the app but only on the sensor itself and the alarm can not be stopped within the app - this makes them less than smart other than their ability to send an alert to your phone. Receiving an alert is important especially when away from home. I use these in conjunction with my security cameras so if one was to go off I can quickly pull up the camera for that area and check activity.

If the app was improved allowing for setting sensitivity and alarm cancellation this would definitely be a 5 star product - even as it is, this is a reasonable product at a decent price.

This is an easy way to add another layer of security to your property without spending too much money. When used in combination with a more advanced security system these are a great addition.

**Please note that this review was written by a novice photographer.
I have been asking my husband for a camera for years. You know how it is....the entire time he is taking pictures with his Nikon D80 (he fancies himself a fantastic photographer...and he is), I am constantly in his ear telling how what I see and envision would make a better picture. I also tell him how he should take a picture of something that I believe will make him the next Ansel Adams. And I complete the photo shoot with, "if only I had really good camera, I would"..... Well, I guess he was tired of hearing it, and decided to buy me this camera (for Christmas thru Amazon) if for no other reason than to shut me up. I guess it was his way of putting "his" money where "my" mouth is, and I was delighted.

Now what is there to like about this camera.
-This camera is user friendly and great for a beginner photographer or at least one that is ready to move from a camera like a Nikon CoolPix. It is perfect for still shots and video (HD). It is easy to select a setting (portrait, action, etc), point and shoot. It focuses automatically (press halfway) and can be manually adjusted (tight or far away photos). There is a menu that allows you to edit and even make images, black and white. **Please note that this is the one feature that no matter how much I read the manual, I can't quite get it to do what I would like. I can edit a picture, change it to black & white, and even use the zoom tool, but when I attempt to save it, it won't. That is a feature that I will have to continue to fool with. And if anyone can help me, I would appreciate it.
-You can manipulate the viewing screen...it flips out and turns (for use while recording video) so that you can view it. Or you can swivel, flip and turn the screen around and collapse it against the body of the camera. This allows you to see or view the pictures you are taking or have taken.
- This camera takes crisp/clear photos. They are amazingly clear.
-This camera has a continuously shoot feature/function. It is great for my son's wrestling matches.
-This camera has an automatic flash that is useful if you aren't sure about the lighting.
-This camera is light (weight wise) enough to carry around for a long period of time (your hand won't get tired), but it also comes with a comfortable and adjustable neck strap. There are also cords that come with the camera so that you can use with the computer or TV.
-The battery life is decent. I assume that it also depends on how many videos you do versus still shots. However, I have done both and found and didn't have a problem. This camera also comes with a convenient battery charger.
Overall, I love my new Canon Rebel T3i and look forward to (a) learning everything about it that I can and (2) taking tons of fantastic pictures for years to come.

Security Warning: All devices from Xiongmai, a Chinese OEM who manufactures white-label video surveillance equipment, come with an always-on cloud feature called XMEye P2P cloud. This feature contains serious vulnerabilities that allow attacks on millions of devices, even ones that are behind firewalls.

Millions of security cameras, DVRs, and NVRs contain vulnerabilities that can allow a remote attacker to take over devices with little effort, security researchers have revealed recently.

All vulnerable devices have been manufactured by Hangzhou Xiongmai Technology Co., Ltd. (often referred to as Xiongmai), a Chinese company based in the city of Hangzhou.

End users won't be able to tell that they're using a hackable device because the company doesn't sell any products with its name on them, but ships all equipment as white label products on which other companies put their logo on top. Evtevision is one of said companies.

If the product description mentions anything about "XMEye," then despite the logo on the front of the device, the equipment was made by Xiongmai.

As you can see in the third bulleted point at the top of the listing:

“Easy view on Smartphone via Xmeye, PC tablet via CMS,and Web browser IE.”

This is, without question, a Xiongmai device. Installing it or any of its software would place the privacy and security of you and your family in serious jeopardy.

Most security companies have banned selling these types of cameras for the reasons I have explained.

I ordered the 'New Sennheiser Momentum Wireless Noise Cancelling Headphones with Auto On/Off, Smart Pause Functionality and Smart Control App' to review. So far, and after almost a month of testing and playing with these amazing headphones, I am ready to share my thoughts.

First and foremost I must express that I am really disappointed in the case that Sennheiser has included with these "High End" Headphones. I mean come on Sennheiser. It seems pretty standard these days for higher end headphones to come with a nice clam-shell hard case. The case provided is a soft zipper pouch with little to no padding at all. I would not feel comfortable to stuff these into my backpack or even suitcase for that matter.

Now with that said, these headphones ARE solid. The stainless steel headband is sturdy and not fragile. The headphones themselves are of a very nice quality construction with real leather, both on the headband and ear pads. The physical buttons (which I tend to like much better than the new "touch" buttons on some of the others out there) are nice and solid and function perfectly.

The sound is absolutely AMAZING! I compared them to my wife's Bose QuietComfort 35 II headphones and honestly I love the sound signature on the Momentum's better. And as for the Noise Cancellation, I honestly can't tell much difference between the two. I do think the Bose do a slightly better job but for the sound quality you get out of the Momentum's, I'll stick with the Momentum's.

As for the weight and comfort compared to the Bose, the Bose are lighter but not necessarily more comfortable. The Momentum's just feel SOLID. The Bose feel nice but light and flimsy.

Other thoughts - Others complain about the "auto pause" feature on the Momentum's, but I personally love it. Others complain about the way you have to power these off by folding them up and personally, it doesn't bother me a bit. I would rather that then pressing a button and wondering if you pressed it correctly. This way, you KNOW they are off.

Battery life isn't the greatest compared to many others in this price range but for me it's just fine. I don't travel long distances and for the occasional 5-6 hour flights I rarely take, they will give me what I need. Plus with the much appreciated USB type C charging port, they will charge pretty fast.

Overall I LOVE everything about these, except for the soft flimsy case provided. Sound is fantastic! They are loud with rich thumping Bass, Nice clean Mids and wonderfully crisp Highs and for me the Sound Isolation works great.

At less than six dollars, I'm happy with this purchase of 2.5" USB 2.0 SATA Hard Drive HDD Case Enclosure.  I was not looking for an incredibly durable case which will be transported much, if at all, so this works fine for me.  All parts were included and the quality is far from great, but it does work and that's what I needed.  My package included two little screwdrivers because perhaps they've found that one is too soft to use for two little bitty screws, but I used another screwdriver anyway.  The black faux whatever case fits snugly, so if you don't use screws on yours, the case can actually be held together.  The silver aluminum is not a heavy gauge, but then again, I don't need a heavy duty case.  Plugging my 80 gig drive (removed from a MacBook) into the end slot, being very careful to not dislodge or mess up anything since it's not real sturdy, careful to hold only the edges of the drive and use a flat table to hold the end cap.  When I first inserted the drive into the case, the opposite end popped out one of the little holes on that end.  I could not get it reattached with the drive inserted, so I removed the drive, placed the reinserted end cap (one without the drive) on the table and gently inserted the drive.  It was not a smooth operation, but took less than a minute.  I then lined up one hole and inserted the screw with only a turn or two.  Lined up the second hole and inserted the second screw, then tightened them both.  Next, I plugged the USB cable into the drive, then inserted the USB which was not an offshoot into the MacBook.  It took a couple attempts for the Mac to accept the drive because it had not properly been ejected when removed from the computer, but after removing it and restarting the computer, it was recognized and accessed right away.  It's been working fine and I'm pleased to have this additional drive now in case it's needed.

The high frequency response of the phones is clear at max volume and the bass is deep (but not thumping). The mid range seems to be the sweet spot, and is rich and full. The volume itself is not super loud, and it is not noise-isolating. It does keep out most ambient noise though, and while these are not perfect for critical listening they are excellent for casual listening during sports and other strenuous activities.

I've always wanted a Canon macro flash but the cost was just too much for something that I would not use very regularly. This macro light, while not a flash, is a very affordable alternative that works very well.

It is a 48 LED light. There's no communication with the camera - it's not a flash, nor can it be controlled in any way by the camera itself. The controls are manual, and allow you to use all the LEDs, half of them (left) or half of them (right). It is powered by 2 AA batteries or by an AC adapter (included). The battery pack mounts on the hotshoe, and the macro light is affixed to the lens barrel.

The battery pack fit fine on my Canon 5D Mark II, but the manufacturer includes a note with the device that says an additional adapter will be needed for it to fit the hotshoe of Sony, Konica and Minolta DSLR cameras.

It comes with two diffusers (white and orange) that are easy to put on and take off. It also comes with six lens thread adapter rings for all the usual sizes - 49mm, 52, 55, 58, 62, and 67. You attach the adapter ring to front of lens, and slot the light over the ring.

No problems fitting it to a Canon L 100mm macro lens. Fit well and was secure during use.

It throws a good amount of light on a ultra close-range subject, which may be otherwise shaded by the close proximity of your lens, or for other reasons be hard to light properly. But, there are limitations - don't expect this to throw a lot of light like a light panel would on a subject at medium distance.

The build quality is better than expected given the price. It's all plastic, but seems more than durable enough for home use.

I'm very pleased with this. It's a small fraction of the cost of a Canon ring light and, while it does not have flash capabilities, it remains a very helpful addition to lighting those tricky macro shots. Highly recommend.

I've tried so many different types of headphones, from very cheap to uber-expensive, and even bluetooth hearing aids trying to listen to music while working or exercising. I've been frustrated (infuriated, really) with most of them. I have very small ears, so most of the over-ear or on-ear headphones I've used have been just way too bulky, hot, and uncomfortable. But the earbuds and earphone-type headphones have been majorly aggravating and just don't sound very good. I did find a pair that stay in my ears, but then I have to remember to charge them repeatedly. Why does it have to be so hard?

Well, it doesn't with these C6 headphones. They are the perfect size for me. After I've had them on for a while, I don't even notice I'm wearing them except when I notice that I am not fatigued from listening. I hadn't realized it until I listened to some of my music with these headphones, but a lot of the headphones I've tried really muddy the sound. A lot of these bass-boosting devices trash all the dynamics and make it difficult to cleanly hear the words and notes played. Some of them even further compress already overly compressed music, which makes for horrible listening fatigue and also risks hearing damage. So when I first put these C6 headphones on, I thought they weren't very good with the bass because of all the other nuances of the music I was able to hear! It didn't take long for me to adjust.

I absolutely love the way these headphones keep the music from being too loud. I've been sitting here listening as I write this, now a few hours into wearing them, and I have absolutely zero fatigue and am really enjoying being able to play album after album. Folk, Rock, Country, Alternative Rock, all sound really good. I'm not an audiophile, but I've done some computer-based recording and sound editing and think these would work very well as monitors. I'm picking up on L-R panning and other sound engineering methods used by various artists that I hadn't realized were there before.

Also, I have to credit these headphones with my discovering Play Music for Chrome. I've been listening to music with Amazon's music player, but under these headphones I thought the music sounded horrid. I realized it was a matter of the acoustical space, so I went out hunting for something that would allow me to add a little reverb. And found that Play Music sounds fantastic with these headphones! I don't know what they are doing differently, but the difference in quality is amazing. And they actually fit on my recliner-desk beside my 15" MacBook Pro, beside my Time Machine backup drive, when I have to take them off for any reason. I love them.

UPDATE: Oh, shoot. I don't know what I did, but I've apparently ruined these headphones. There are small wires extending from the headset part to the ear cups, and I must have tugged on one of the cords enough to short something out. This resulted in my losing the high mids and frequencies above it. I went to the site myNoise dot net and tried to calibrate to these headphones, and there was literally nothing there in the top three sliders. I might have questioned if it was hearing loss (which I do have), except my other headphones don't completely lose those frequencies. Bummer. I was so happy with them. I had to knock off a star.

Philips Magnavox PR1903C is a simple television set designed for the technologically apathetic. It has very few features and very few of the mechanical and technological updates one would expect in a modern television.

This television set offers the usual minimum features a consumer expects to find in any television- like adjustments for color, brightness, etc.- along with a few extras, like a language control that allows the consumer to switch from English to Spanish to French, sleep timer, and close captioning. Most all features have to be accessed from the remote control- the front of the television offers no such options- not even to access the menu. Also, there is only one input jack on the back of the television, placing severe limits on accessory compatibility.

If there is one redeeming factor for this television set, it is the quality of the picture.

This surprised me at first, because the overall quality of most everything else is below average, leading me to believe that the picture quality would follow suit. But the picture is actually quite good on Philips Magnavox PR1903C. The sharpness is very good and I cannot detect any small lines or other problems with the viewing. In this regard, the television set deserves commendation. I can't really find anything wrong with the picture quality for this type of set.

Going back to the negative points, I have noticed that this television set is prone to wear out a little faster than others. One sign of wear that is easily noticeable is the button on the front of the screen, to access the power. This button is a large, round button that is plastic in construction and is enclosed inside a round space. When pressing the button in, it is supposed to snap solidly in place but instead it rattles back and forth a little, making me worry that it is going to pop off. Of course, the way it is situated inside the round space, it cannot come out (as far as I know). But the looseness is obvious and it is a little surprising. With the limited amount of times the power button on the front of the television set is used (it is usually powered on/off with the remote control), I wouldn't expect it to wear out so quickly.

Overall, Philips Magnavox PR1903C is an unacceptable television set for the many reasons listed above. I like the sleep timer and the picture quality is certainly very good, but the strikes against this television are numerous. There are too many bad points to make it worthy of a recommendation.

I bought an Atoto F7 standard last summer, and while I loved the features for the price, there were some shortcomings that made me want to try their higher end S8 editions instead. I got a chance to swap it out for an S8 Ultra, and I'm very impressed so far.
Let me tell you, I had my reservations about a phone/tablet OS running as a car stereo, but Atoto has done an incredible job making this as smooth and user friendly and FEATURE PACKED as you could ever imagine. Android Auto works of course, if you want to use your phone connected to the display. Even better, WIRELESS Android Auto works as well! They don't advertise this since it is in beta as of the time I'm writing this, but after asking Atoto customer support about it I was given access to the new test firmware and it works surprisingly well with my Galaxy S10 phone. All I have to do is press the Carlink button on the screen, my phone can stay in my pocket, and within 10-15 seconds the Android Auto connection is displayed on the car screen as if I had plugged it in. It also has an excellent Bluetooth audio input for the microphone, which is something I struggled with on the F7 I purchased previously. My car has a convertible roof that creates extra wind noise on the highway even closed, and callers can hear me just fine! But of course, the biggest pro is the ability to run Android apps directly on the head unit without needing to connect my phone.
I preloaded offline maps for most of NY/NJ in Google Maps, so wherever I end up I can navigate home (even if I don't have reception up in the mountains), all without needing my phone connected. I can also stream youtube and other apps (for the passengers, obviously!) as well as install all kinds of cool automation tools and car diagnostics thanks to a bluetooth OBDii plug I already owned.

It's not without a few caveats, however. Some things to be aware of:
1) The unit has a 5 minute delay when shutting off. This is apparently to avoid data corruption in case of a power cycle (key removed and restarted, such as for example if restarting the car). If you plug anything into the USB ports, you'll see them still on and drawing power for a solid 5 minutes after you've left the car. My wireless charger, for example, continues to be lit up and charging if I use the head unit's QuickCharge port built in. Any other peripherals such as remotes or volume knobs, etc, will remain illuminated for those few minutes. While most apps (built in music player, youtube, etc) are able to receive the signal to stop playing when the power is shut off right away, third party apps (such as some podcast or other streaming music players) actually CONTINUE TO PLAY during this 5 minute delay unless you paused/stopped them before removing the key. It's only a few minutes, and the truth is I usually play podcasts from my phone streaming, which DOES shut off right away since the Bluetooth connection is severed immediately when the key is removed. However I was surprised to find out it didn't stop everything immediately and they don't tell you this in the instructions at all.
2) If you are using Wireless Android Auto / Carplay, it creates a wifi ad-hoc connection that your phone connects to. With Android Auto, this can take a pretty big hit off your battery, but it is worth it to not pull your phone out on a small drive. However, due to the 5 minute delay I mentioned earlier, you might find that your phone is still connected to the car for a few minutes after you've left if you are in proximity of it. My car is parked just outside my office window, so I was surprised my phone wasn't connecting to my office wifi at first, then a few minutes later the car finally shut off the wifi and my phone was able to connect to the local network as expected. That delay, once again, was a little bit unexpected since at first I did not understand what was wrong.
3) Bluetooth and Android Auto volume are not consistent. For some reason, when connected with Android Auto, the volume is louder. So if you switch between them you'll have to adjust. Again, none of these are deal breakers, but things I found odd.
4) Bluetooth streaming has limited control over track. This is the one that surprised me the most since the less expensive F7 is superior in this regard. For those who know about Bluetooth profiles, there's the streaming stereo profile which gives you some ID tag metadata, and then there's AVRCP, which is the part used for remote controlling the playback. It seems that if you're playing audio from a phone, you are only getting the first profile, and not the AVRCP one. I've included a picture to illustrate the difference. With track control like you get on a dedicated bluetooth headunits, it shows the duration of the file being played, and you can even scrub through it by holding the forward and reverse buttons (like you would on an old school CD player). I listen to a lot of audiobooks so I like seeing how far into the file I am. But on the S8, it just shows the name of the file and artist/title, and then dancing lines to the audio levels. To be honest, the dancing lines are kind of distracting as well, but I can just hit home to go back to the main screen and not look at them. There's not much point in staying on that screen if I don't get track duration info anyway.

All in all, I think these setbacks are largely due to the way Android works and was designed as an OS. I think these limitations are reasonable. Atoto support has been amazing and incredibly responsive, whenever I had a question or concern, they got back to me within 24 hours which is more than I can say about radios I've owned from Pioneer and Sony in the past.

I was looking for some replacement headphones for two sets in my family when I had the opportunity to try out some of the new Carlos Santana line of headphones. Let's see what happened.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These headphones come in a great box which will appeal to fans of Carlose. It is well decorated and presentation is done so well, it would make a great gift. These are the black ones, and there is also another set available in white under a different listing.

ARE THESE REAL LEATHER?
According to the case,t these are leather padded ear cups and the lower half of the headband. I am still not sure about this. It is possibly bonded leather. Bonded leather is made from leather scraps chopped up and blended with binders. Sheets made of this mixture are printed with leather look imprinting. Technically it can be called leather, but it really is not leather as I define it..

EAR CUSHIONS AND HEADBAND
These black headphones are comfortable. I can wear these headphones longer than many others I have used. My daughter who ended up with these, uses them constantly and raves about them. These can be worn for several hours without a problem. She has sweaty ears and these are not nearly as frustrating for her as many others.

CORD FOR CORDED LISTENING
This comes with a cord which is only 38 inches long. That is a bit short for me. I find it is annoying and not quite as long as I would prefer, but my daughter does not use it so I guess it is not a problem for her or if you are like her, you won't mind either.

HOW DO THESE SOUND?
We are all surprised at how really good these sound. The bass is well defined and clear/strong, and the mids and highs are definitely clear and not muddy. The bass is not overwhelming either, which is a problem with some headphones.

HEADPHONE CONTROLS
The controls can be a bit difficult to read, but once you know where they are, you can figure it out pretty quickly. The +/- and play/pause buttons are separated by the noise cancellation button which is good.

HOW ARE THESE ADJUSTABLE?
These adapt to all sorts of comfortable positions.. They go longer, tilt in and out and rotate from side to side.

ARE THESE ABLE TO FOLD TO BE COMPACT?
These do fold flat and compact if you need to travel with them or store them in a smaller storage area.

CASE?
This did not come with a case.

SOUND CANCELLATION PERFORMANCE
The noise cancellation is awful. It hardly works. When noise cancellation is turned on, the sound gets pretty compromised. It becomes almost muffled in a way and the base definitely goes down.

OTHER FEATURES WITH THESE HEADPHONES
The ability to know how much power is left on the headphones while using the phone is nice, but it does not help if you are using these some other bluetooth device and not a phone. During phone calls, people hear just fine and we can hear them too (several of us tried this feature with our phones)

THE BOTTOM LINE
At this price point, these headphones are a step up from what I usually get when getting headphones for this price range. The sound is well defined and well balanced. Compactness for storage is great, and the comfort is also very good. The only disappointments are noise cancellation, short cord for corded listening, and buttons being a bit difficult to read.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. With better performance from noise cancellation, these would be really really good. As they are, they are still pretty great. They are a great gift to yourself or someone else and are some of the nicer headphones I have used in my journey through headphones of all sorts as well as those the family has obtained. They are not B&O or Turtle Beach, but they still are pretty good.
